comments.author: jedberg
comments.text:
I would love to see these benchmarks split up across "generic" tasks and novel tasks.
For example, redlining an OEM agreement with my vendor.  They pretty much all use the same template, and the objections are always the same.  I tried using Claude first, and even my lawyer was impressed that it found things they missed.  Then I used Claude to redline that type of contract and the other side said "your lawyer was surprisingly thorough".  I had my lawyer do the final check, but saved a bunch of money doing the first three rounds with Claude instead.  And my lawyer basically just said "looks good to me" by the time they reviewed it.
Or even writing a simple will or estate document.
It seems like LLMs are great for the kind of generic work you'd usually pawn off to a new associate or paralegal, but not for the important things that partners usually do.

comments.author: victor9000

I’m not sure if this is the right solution, but we clearly need better tools for the legal space.  Anthropic's recent policy update makes this abundantly clear:
“When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified ‘human in the loop’ (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.”
Something as common as a family law case has the potential to affect all of the above.  Now imagine being a petitioner, respondent, paralegal, or other 3rd party using Claude to review a draft document only to find out that Anthropic has sent your entire file to opposing counsel.
It sounds egregious, but Anthropic is clearly stating they will use their own judgment to control what people can do with its product, and that they will treat customer data as if it's theirs to disseminate.  So there's a massive opportunity for an unbiased tool willing to fill this void.

comments.author: pbsd
comments.text:
An old version of binutils [1] explains what DDS means:
How to encode VEX.vvvv:
0: VEX.vvvv must be 1111b.
1: VEX.NDS.  Register-only source is encoded in VEX.vvvv where
the content of source registers will be preserved.
VEX.DDS.  The second register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv
where the content of first source register will be overwritten
by the result.
VEX.NDD2.  The second destination register operand is encoded in
VEX.vvvv for instructions with 2 destination register operands.
For assembler, there are no difference between VEX.NDS, VEX.DDS
and VEX.NDD2.
2. VEX.NDD.  Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv for
instructions with 1 destination register operand.
3. VEX.LWP.  Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv and one
of the operands can access a memory location.
[1]
https://sourceware.org/git/?p=binutils-gdb.git;a=commitdiff;...

It only existed in SDM volume 2 revisions 082 to 084. It did not appear in #252046, the changes doc -- so its existence in volume 2 was not intentional.

The way I have to resume downloads in Firefox is
1. Move the .part file to a temp file

comments.author: select1dev
comments.text:
I run a daily job that clones and runs a freshly launched open-source project in a sandbox, so a few notes from the consumer side of this market.
Your point about bursty CPU matches what I see: install and build spike for 20–60 seconds, then the process mostly idles while the harness reads output. RAM only matters the day a project pulls in a headless browser.
The things that actually cost me time were not CPU or RAM, though. First, network policy. I run untrusted code with an egress allowlist, and most launched projects assume open internet, so the useful knob is per-sandbox allowlist editing with a proxy for package registries, not more memory. Second, environment hygiene. The sandbox needs a clean env with no inherited secrets, and a persistent sandbox that does not pick up changed env vars or allowlist entries without a restart bit me more than once. Third, a wall-clock timebox per run, because a stuck npm install behind a proxy fails silently rather than loudly.
Two questions: can a sandbox’s egress allowlist be changed while it is running, and when gVisor does not support a workload (you mention Docker-in-Docker), does the API fail fast or does the job just hang?

comments.author: pathly
comments.text:
This is really impressive work on the infrastructure side.
Skipping hyperscalers like AWS for Hetzner/OVH is definitely a massive lever, but your choice of gVisor for memory overcommit is where this gets technically interesting. A few questions on the implementation:
• Memory & Density: Since gVisor allows you to share memory without reserving a full VM's allocation, how are you handling noisy neighbors if multiple sandboxes spike in RAM usage simultaneously? Are you using specific cgroups configurations or out-of-memory (OOM) killer tuning to prevent one sandbox from crashing the host?
• Storage Persistence: You mentioned that files stay with the agent across sessions. How are you handling the storage layer efficiently at $0.05–$0.10/user? Are you using localized NVMe storage with networked backups, or something like ceph/block storage?
• Cold Starts: When a sandbox wakes up from auto-sleep, what is the exact latency for the user?
Congrats on the launch and the pivot from a simple wrapper to a real infrastructure play!

The inverters follow the grid AC and shut off their output if they are disconnected or unplugged, so the plug is never "hot". The power they input into your home wiring/the power grid is limited to 800 Watts as to not overload any installation. And the power meters know not to run backwards if you happen to feed power into the grid. Most can even meter how much power you fed in total (you're not going to get paid for it, though)
If you want, you can add battery storage that follows the same rules but lets you save excess power during the day to feed into your home at night or during demand spikes (washing machine, ...).

stories.title_en: Were Software Engineers blue-collar workers all along?

comments.author: Autious
comments.text:
I don't lament LLM's because they are a better or automation of an approach to doing my tasks. I lament them because they are built on loose foundations, limited understanding, misunderstood function and risk, data theft, and shaky legal grounds. I'm an engineer, my job is to deal with and reduce complexity not accept it blindly without soberly weighing all the pros and cons after building a solid understanding.
We also don't know how this approach will pan out and the extent of its final functionality. Some people think it'll just get better, but nothing in the world scales linearly forever, why would this?
We will likely construct a general solution machine one day and help us create resource abundance, and with that lead to a world where we can work on a completely new foundation of a human philosophy and social structure to live in, but there's no guarantee we're on that path with this garbage, and it's a moral failure to just accept that we are and deem ourselves replaced prematurely.

[features]
